title: Haloform reaction: the C–C cleavage
subtitle: Hydroxide adds, and CBr₃⁻ is the leaving group

reactants.caption: 1,1,1-tribromoacetone + sodium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: The three brominations are done. Hydroxide now attacks: draw the first step of the cleavage.
hintTiers: Three bromines make the carbonyl group very electrophilic. Hydroxide is the nucleophile. Where does it add?
Hydroxide adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → a new bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon, not a bromine atom.
An SN2 at a carbon carrying three bromines is blocked: the bromines shield its back face. The carbonyl carbon is the electrophile.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydroxide bonds to the carbonyl carbon. That carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π electrons onto oxygen.

tetrahedral.caption: the tetrahedral intermediate
tetrahedral.learnerPrompt: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses. Which group leaves?
hintTiers: The O⁻ lone pair re-forms C=O, and one group on the carbon must leave. Which carbanion is stabilised enough to leave?
The C–CBr₃ bond breaks: three bromines stabilise the carbanion (CHBr₃ has a pKa of about 14). Two arrows.
Oxygen lone pair → a π bond back to the carbon; the bond to the CBr₃ carbon → a lone pair on that carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: CH₃⁻ is far too unstable to leave (pKa of methane about 50). The CBr₃⁻ anion is stabilised by three bromines.
Hydroxide leaving just goes back to the ketone. Here the carbanion CBr₃⁻ can leave too, and that step is not reversed.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: CBr₃⁻ leaves. The carbonyl carbon is now short of electrons: push the oxygen lone pair in to re-form C=O.

acid-and-carbanion.caption: acetic acid + tribromomethyl anion
hintTiers: A carboxylic acid (pKa about 5) sits next to a strong base. Which proton moves?
The CBr₃⁻ carbon takes the proton from the acid's OH. Two arrows.
Carbanion lone pair → the hydrogen of the OH group; that O–H bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding back to the carbonyl carbon reverses the cleavage. The carbanion is a base: the acid's proton is right beside it.
The oxygen atoms are electron-rich. The carbanion takes the δ+ hydrogen of the OH group.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the carbanion takes the proton. Now break the O–H bond onto oxygen.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The same addition as in ester hydrolysis. The electron-withdrawing CBr₃ group makes this carbonyl carbon unusually electrophilic.
A carbon leaving group is rare. CBr₃⁻ can leave because three bromines pull the negative charge onto themselves: here the ketone behaves like an acid derivative.
The acid (pKa about 5) protonates the carbanion (pKa about 14). This step cannot be reversed, so it pulls the whole reaction to the carboxylate and bromoform.

mechanismSummary: In base a methyl ketone is brominated three times on the methyl group: each bromine makes the remaining α-hydrogens more acidic, so the reaction does not stop. Hydroxide then adds to the carbonyl group of the tribromomethyl ketone, the tetrahedral intermediate expels CBr₃⁻ (stabilised by three bromines), and a proton transfer gives the carboxylate and bromoform. With iodine, the yellow precipitate of iodoform is the classical test for a methyl ketone.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20
